name: Miksa Róth Memorial House and Collection
intro: The Róth Miksa Emlékház és Gyűjtemény is a small museum in the former home and workshop of Miksa Róth, one of Hungary’s best-known glass painters and mosaic makers. Visitors find a preserved family apartment and an exhibition of his mosaics and glass in the street building, while his large workshop still stands in the courtyard behind.
about: The museum occupies the house at Nefelejcs utca 26 in Erzsébetváros, the building the Róth family moved into in 1911. The museum’s own website describes the street-front house as the former family home and notes that Róth’s large workshop building still survives in the old yard behind it. The institution is presented as part of the KULT7 group.

There are two permanent displays upstairs. The Lakásmúzeum, or apartment museum, shows rooms that recreate how an upper-middle-class household lived in the early 1900s, furnished with artworks and personal belongings of the family. The Mozaikok és üvegek exhibition presents a selection of Róth’s mosaic and glass work and looks at the symbolism and material innovations in it. The museum highlights his collaboration with the Zsolnay factory and an award-winning mosaic, made with Tiffany glass, that won a silver medal at the Paris World’s Fair.

The official site also lists a temporary chamber exhibition called RÓTH160. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that the ground floor has a temporary exhibition hall and a salon made from Róth’s former study, and that the former workshop shows works by his students and followers; because layouts change, check the museum’s website for what is currently on show.
The museum’s directions use the Keleti pályaudvar stop, which makes it easy to pair with a visit to the station. Its programme page has listed English-language guided tours on some dates.
tips: Check the museum’s official website before you go for the current exhibitions, visiting arrangements, ticket information and any English-language guided tours.
The museum’s directions page gives the Keleti pályaudvar stop, served by metro lines 2 and 4, as the main way to arrive; the museum itself has no car park.
The museum states that the building has no lift, so ask in advance if stairs are a problem.

Keleti station and its large train hall are close by, and the connection is more than geographic: Samu Pecz, who remodelled Róth’s house, also designed the Unitarian church on Nagy Ignác utca, whose rose window was glazed in Róth’s workshop.

history.intro: Miksa Róth lived and worked in this house for decades, and the story of the building runs from a master’s workshop through wartime and communist-era institutions to a museum opened in 1999.

sections.heading: A glass painter from a glassmaking family
paragraphs: According to the museum, Miksa Róth was born in Pest in 1865 into a family with a glasswork tradition and died in 1944. By the age of twenty he was working as an independent artist. He is described as a leading figure of glass painting and mosaic art and as a central figure of the Hungarian Secession, and he held the title of Royal Court Glass Painter, awarded by Emperor and King Franz Joseph.

The museum notes gold and silver medals at world’s fairs and public-building commissions in Mexico, the Netherlands and Norway, as well as many Budapest works that still decorate the city. The parish of the Unitarian church on Nagy Ignác utca records that the glazing of its rose window came from his workshop.

sections.heading: The house at Nefelejcs utca
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says the house first belonged to a furniture manufacturer, Sámuel Gelb. Róth bought it in 1911 and had it remodelled to plans by Samu Pecz, and a three-storey workshop building was added in the courtyard. The article gives 1911 to 1944 as the years in which the buildings were his home and workshop.

After Róth died in 1944 the property was soon nationalised. The same article records that a German and then a Soviet military cartography office used the buildings during the Second World War and that a military academy for political officers worked there from 1948; the building then deteriorated, and part of it later served as an industrial workshop and as emergency housing.

sections.heading: From family rooms to museum
paragraphs: The museum says Róth’s widow and some of the children kept living in parts of the building. Plans to turn the house and its heritage into a museum took shape in the 1990s, and the former family home received its licence as the Róth Miksa Emlékház és Gyűjtemény in 1999.

Hungarian Wikipedia adds that after the political change the family donated the artist’s estate to the Erzsébetváros district, partly through the mediation of Mihály Ráday, and that the museum opened in November 1999 after a long preparation.

name: National Theatre
intro: The Nemzeti Színház, Hungary’s National Theatre, occupies a building on the Pest bank of the Danube that opened on 15 March 2002 with a performance of Imre Madách’s The Tragedy of Man. Mária Siklós’s design pairs a rounded main auditorium with public areas, a U-shaped service wing and a landscaped park.
about: The National Theatre stands at Bajor Gizi park 1 in Ferencváros, on the Danube embankment next to the Müpa arts complex. It is a working repertory theatre: its programme page lists Hungarian classics such as Bánk bán and Csongor és Tünde alongside Our Town, and the house hosts the Madách International Theatre Meeting, a festival founded in 2014.

According to the theatre, the building has three functional parts: a central section with a nearly circular auditorium and a studio stage, public areas around it, and a U-shaped service wing wrapped around the main stage. The main stage seats 619, the Gobbi Hilda Stage seats about 150 on movable seating, and an open-air stage faces the Danube. The foyer rises through the full height of the building, two panoramic lifts serve it, and the upper galleries have views of the river and the Buda Hills.

The theatre sits in landscaped parkland, which its own description treats as part of the building. The website mentions a garden and sculpture park, a relief honouring the actor Attila Kaszás by Sándor Krisztiáni and a Trianon memorial in the so-called Hajóorr, or ship’s prow. The main entrance faces Gellért Hill across the water.

English Wikipedia notes that the Müpa, the Palace of Arts, opened next door in 2005, so the park and embankment form a small cultural cluster on the riverside. A visit works best as an evening at the theatre, perhaps with a walk along the embankment before or after.
tips: Check the theatre’s official website, which also has an English version, for the current programme, performance languages and ticketing; do not assume that a production is available in English.

The theatre’s own directions name trams 2 and 24 to the Müpa – Nemzeti Színház stop, the first stop of the Csepel HÉV line from Boráros tér, and buses 23, 54 and 55; confirm current routes before you travel.
The theatre offers guided tours of the building for groups, see its visiting page for how to ask.
The Müpa, the Danube embankment and the Pest end of Rákóczi Bridge are all next to the park, so the surroundings are worth a short walk before or after an evening here.

history.intro: The company is much older than its building: it was founded in the 1830s and spent more than a century in borrowed or temporary homes before it moved into the present house on the Danube.

sections.heading: Founding in Pest, 1832 to 1840
paragraphs: The theatre’s own history credits Count István Széchenyi with proposing a large theatre building in a pamphlet of 1832. The Hungarian Diet passed Act XLI of 1836, which ordered a national theatre in Pest, and the theatre opened on 22 August 1837 as the Pesti Magyar Színház, the Pest Hungarian Theatre. It took the name Nemzeti Színház in 1840.
The first building stood at the corner of Rákóczi út and Múzeum körút. It was enlarged in 1875, closed in 1908 for safety reasons and demolished between October 1913 and March 1914.

sections.heading: Years of temporary homes
paragraphs: From 1908 the company rented the Népszínház on Blaha Lujza tér. Its demolition was announced in 1963 because of metro construction; the last performance was on 28 June 1964 and the building was blown up in 1965. The company then played at Nagymező utca 22 from 1964, where the Thália Színház now stands, and moved on 1 October 1966 to the former Magyar Színház on Hevesi Sándor tér, where it stayed for 34 years.

sections.heading: A new building on the Danube
paragraphs: Plans for a purpose-built house were long and troubled. The theatre’s history says Ferenc Bán won a design competition for a site on Erzsébet tér in 1997 and that a foundation stone was laid there in 1998, but work stopped that September. English Wikipedia dates Bán’s win a year earlier; the sources differ on that detail.

In 1999 Mária Siklós was commissioned to design a new building and the Ferencváros riverside site was chosen. Construction began on 14 September 2000 and took about fifteen months; rehearsals started on 2 January 2002, and the house opened on 15 March 2002, Hungary’s national day, with Madách’s The Tragedy of Man.

name: Keleti Railway Station
intro: Budapest-Keleti is the city’s main international and inter-city railway terminus, an eclectic station that opened on 16 August 1884 on Baross tér. Chief engineer Gyula Rochlitz designed the building and bridge engineer János Feketeházy its iron structure, and the station remains a working hub for domestic and international trains.
about: Keleti pályaudvar stands at the head of Baross tér in Józsefváros, at Kerepesi út 2-4. It is a station that most people pass through rather than visit, but the building is worth a look. The name means Eastern Station and refers to its position and to the lines it served towards Transylvania and the Balkans.

Hungarian Wikipedia describes a main facade 43 metres high, topped by an allegorical sculpture group by Gyula Bezerédi that was re-cast in the 1990s reconstruction. Statues of James Watt and George Stephenson flank the main entrance. Behind the facade the iron-framed hall, which the same article gives as 42 metres wide, spans the platforms, and the ticket hall has frescoes by Károly Lotz and Mór Than.

In front of the station the square carries a statue of Gábor Baross, unveiled in 1898 in the middle of Baross tér. It was moved to the north side of the hall during the 1968 redevelopment and returned to its original position in December 2013. Beneath the square, the station is the meeting point of metro lines M2 and M4.
MÁV’s station page lists domestic and international ticket offices, a lost-property office, left-luggage lockers near the Utascentrum at underpass level, a lift, waiting rooms and nearby parking.
tips: Check MÁV’s station page and the track-closure news before you travel, since platforms, works and services change.

To enjoy the building without a ticket, look at the facade and statues from Baross tér and then step inside to see the hall and the ticket hall frescoes; keep luggage in sight, as at any large terminus.
Metro lines M2 and M4 meet at the station, which makes it a convenient place to change between rail and the city’s metro.
The Miksa Róth Memorial House on Nefelejcs utca uses the Keleti pályaudvar stop in its own directions, so the two can be combined in one outing.

history.intro: Keleti was built in the early 1880s as the capital’s central terminus and has been rebuilt, repaired and renovated several times since, while keeping its original role.

sections.heading: Building a terminus on soft ground
paragraphs: According to Hungarian Wikipedia, a decision to build a new central station was taken in 1880 and the site at the Kerepesi road customs post, where Baross tér now lies, was marked out in November 1881. The state railways built it to Gyula Rochlitz’s design with the steel hall structure by János Feketeházy, in eclectic style; the article says it was modelled on the old Berlin main station. Groundwater about a metre down required roughly 3,000 piles, which is why it was not finished in 1883 as planned.

The station opened on 16 August 1884. MÁV recalls that the first train left that day for Miskolc and that the first passengers arrived from Ruttka and Zimony, and quotes the Budapesti Hírlap of that date praising a building that was rarely matched far and wide.

sections.heading: From Központi to Keleti
paragraphs: The station was first called the Központi Pályaudvar, the Central Station. Hungarian Wikipedia says that a decree of 20 September 1892 renamed it Budapest-Keleti after the state railways absorbed another company, which left the word central meaningless. Overhead electrification followed in 1931.

MÁV lists trains with a place in Hungarian railway history that began their journeys here, among them the Kandó locomotive V 40 001, the diesel railcar Árpád to Vienna and the Orient Express towards the Balkans. The station was severely damaged by bombing in the Second World War.

sections.heading: Rebuilt square, restored hall
paragraphs: The square in front was rebuilt in 1967 to 1970 for the M2 metro, which reached the station in 1970; English Wikipedia notes that M4 arrived in 2014 after a decade of works on the forecourt. According to Hungarian Wikipedia the facade and hall were renovated in 2002 and 2004, four statues lost in the 1930s were replaced in 2003, and the underpass renovation was completed in May 2023.

seo.title: Keleti Railway Station, Budapest
seo.description: Budapest-Keleti, the city’s main international rail terminus opened in 1884: its eclectic facade, iron hall, Baross tér and how its history unfolded.

name: Buda Arboretum
address: Villányi út 29-43, 1118 Budapest (southern foot of Gellért Hill)
intro: The Budai Arborétum is a historic teaching garden of about 7.5 hectares at the southern foot of Gellért Hill, run by the Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences. Planting began in 1893 and 1894, and Ménesi út divides it into an Upper and a Lower Garden with nearly 2,000 woody ornamental species and cultivars.
about: The Buda Arboretum belongs to the university’s Budai Campus on Villányi út in the eleventh district. According to the arboretum’s own introduction it is one of the richest arboreta in Hungary and serves as a teaching garden for horticulture students, as well as a place where newly introduced woody plants are tested. The site’s warm microclimate lets many southern plants thrive.

Ménesi út cuts the garden in two. The Upper Garden lies on the steeper slope above the road and is known for old, rare trees, including what the arboretum calls the country’s oldest Persian ironwood and a Lebanon oak. The Lower Garden levels out towards Villányi út and holds themed collections: Mediterranean plants, shade-lovers, flowering ornamental trees and species with autumn colour. The height difference across the site is about 80 metres.

The seasons shape a visit. The arboretum says the Lebanon oak, bitternut hickory and ginkgo turn golden in autumn, that fig and Asian persimmon fruit regularly, and that Chinese windmill palms grow in sheltered corners by the buildings. The garden has been a protected natural area since 1975, and the arboretum states that its gardens, buildings and sculptures are listed as historic monuments.
The arboretum is only a short walk from Móricz Zsigmond körtér, so it fits easily with a day on Gellért Hill or in Újbuda.
tips: Check the arboretum’s official website for current visiting arrangements, entrances and its visitor rules; see the official site for what applies in each season.

The official directions name trams 17 and 61 to the Tas vezér utca stop, bus 27 for the Szüret utca and Ménesi út stops, and describe a walk of about five minutes from Móricz Zsigmond körtér. Parking in the area is limited, and the campus offers none for visitors.

Under the posted rules, dogs and other animals, bicycles, scooters and similar vehicles are not allowed in, and visitors are asked to keep to marked paths, leave plants untouched and avoid sitting on the lawns.
Commercial photography or filming, including wedding shoots, needs permission from the staff in advance; ordinary visitors should still avoid picking or collecting anything.
Nearby places to combine it with include Gellért Hill and the Gellért Thermal Bath.

history.intro: The garden grew out of a horticultural training school, and the sources do not agree on every early date, but its main planting began in 1893 and 1894.

sections.heading: A horticultural school on Gellért Hill
paragraphs: The arboretum’s history page says the institute was founded in 1853 thanks to Dr Ferenc Entz, a physician of the 1848–49 War of Independence, and moved to the southern slope of Gellért Hill in 1876. Its first teaching building was the present E building above Ménesi út, once a wine-press house, and the arboretum was laid out around these buildings among old vineyard terraces.

Hungarian Wikipedia gives different dates for the early institution: it says the training institute began operating in the Upper Garden on 2 June 1860 and became state property in 1881. The origin of the institute is therefore dated differently by the two sources.

sections.heading: Räde’s planting and the 1920s extension
paragraphs: Planting of the Upper Garden began in the winter of 1893 and 1894, according to the arboretum, to designs by the German-born gardener and dendrologist Károly Räde (1864–1946), who became its first director. About 1,000 tree and shrub species and 90 perennials were set out on roughly three hectares in a landscape style, grouped by plant family for teaching.

In the late 1920s the garden grew by about three quarters of a hectare under plans by the architect and garden designer Béla Rerrich, with construction supervised by Gyula Magyar. A surviving catalogue lists 1,370 woody taxa, but many rare plants did not cope with cold winters and dry summers, and only about 800 remained by the 1950s.

sections.heading: War damage, restoration and protection
paragraphs: The siege of Budapest turned the garden into a battleground, and the arboretum says bullet marks and shrapnel are still visible on some old trunks. Restoration began in 1949 under Dr Mihály Nádasi. In 1969 about half a hectare of the Upper Garden was taken for a student dormitory and sports facilities.

The Lower Garden, once the institute’s nursery with greenhouses and field crops, became an arboretum in stages after the war. Gábor Schmidt directed the garden from 1974 to 2012, the lower greenhouse for tropical and subtropical plants was built in 1994, and the garden pond followed in 1997. Hungarian Wikipedia records that the area was declared a locally protected natural area in 1975.

name: Unitarian Church, Nagy Ignác utca
intro: The Budapesti Unitárius Templom at Nagy Ignác utca 2-4 is a neo-Gothic brick complex in Lipótváros, designed by Samu Pecz and consecrated on 26 October 1890. The church itself occupies the upper floor of a building with commercial premises below, and its street front is marked by a large rose window and an octagonal copper-clad tower.
about: This is the church of the Budapest Unitarian parish, the Budapesti Unitárius Egyházközség, which gathers under the motto Egy az Isten, One is God. The building also houses the parish office, according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The congregation traces its beginnings to 1869 and has worshipped in this building since its consecration.

The parish describes the complex as three storeys of French-inspired neo-Gothic, built with shops, a café and a restaurant on the ground floor. The church lies on the second floor and is entered from Nagy Ignác utca, formerly Koháry utca, up a two-sided neo-Gothic staircase. The street facade has a large decorative rose window and an octagonal, copper-clad tower known as the hussar tower.

Inside, the church is a single nave about 8 metres wide and 26 metres long, oriented east to west with a five-sided apse at the west end. It has coloured leaded-glass windows; the glazing of the rose window came from the workshop of Miksa Róth. Samu Pecz designed the interior fittings without charge, and Endre Thék made the hardwood pulpit, pews, communion table and a 50-seat gallery on columns. The organ case was carved by the sculptor István Trögl, and the church seats between 350 and 400 people.

The church stands in Lipótváros, the Pest district around the Basilica and Parliament. The parish presents the building as its living church, and its own website is the best place to learn about services, concerts and any arrangements for visitors.
tips: This is a working place of worship, so dress and behave accordingly, and check the parish website for visiting arrangements and for events, as visits depend on what the congregation is doing.
The church is on the second floor, up a staircase from the street, so ask the parish about access if stairs are a concern.
From the pavement, look up at the rose window and the hussar tower; the tower was restored to its original shape and finial in 2013 and 2014.
St Stephen’s Basilica and the Hungarian Parliament are both in Lipótváros and make a natural next stop.

history.intro: The church was built for a young congregation that had waited two decades for a home, and it was financed through an unusual arrangement with a Vienna construction firm.

sections.heading: A congregation without a church
paragraphs: The parish says Unitarian worship became possible in Budapest after 1867. In 1869 the Kolozsvár Unitarian preacher József Ferencz held the first Unitarian service in the capital, which marks the congregation’s beginning. It was formally founded in 1876 as a branch of the Kolozsvár church and became an independent parish in 1881, with Károly Derzsi as its first pastor, who led the fundraising.
In 1883 the Budapest city council donated a plot of 600 square fathoms to the congregation.

sections.heading: Pecz Samu’s design and the 1890 consecration
paragraphs: In 1885 Samu Pecz, then a university professor, was commissioned to design a three-storey complex. In 1888 the Vienna firm Holtzspach-Majorossy offered to build the church and an apartment building in return for the right to use the rented part, the shops, café and flats, for 50 years from 1890 to 1940, a right the congregation could buy out. Pecz prepared the final plans and supervised the building work.
Construction ran from 1888 to 1890 and the church was consecrated on 26 October 1890. The parish adds that Pecz joined the Unitarian church after the building was finished.

sections.heading: War damage, nationalisation and restoration
paragraphs: The building was damaged in 1944: the hussar tower was temporarily repaired and the organ was destroyed. The communist government nationalised the building in 1949, though the congregation kept using it. The parish regained 51 per cent ownership in 1991 and the remaining 49 per cent in 2010.

The facade was restored between 1998 and 2004, and in 2013 and 2014 the roof was re-covered and the tower restored. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that a new organ was installed in 1995 and modernised in 2012.

sources.label: Hungarian Wikipedia: Unitárius templom és székház (Budapest)

seo.title: Unitarian Church, Nagy Ignác utca
seo.description: The neo-Gothic Unitarian church in Lipótváros, designed by Samu Pecz and consecrated in 1890: its rose window, hussar tower and the congregation’s history.
